chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: What Louis Armstrong was like off the bandstand
summary: Crawford describes Armstrong as jovial and generous, says he rarely played with him, and rejects any Uncle Tom image.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well now, getting back to Armstrong, did you -- how well did you know him?
Know him? I knew Louis Armstrong pretty well, very well. Big Sid Catlett -- one of the greatest --
What kind of a person did you find Armstrong to be?

Oh, jovial, always happy, trying to make other people happy, give you the shirt off his back, and foremost one of the greatest trumpet players -- he wasn't as fast as Diz, but he knew what to do with that horn. He played clear, clean notes and worked his brains out. He just was a natural player. That's all.
Did you play with him much?
No, I didn't. Big Sid Catlett was his drummer. I didn't play too much with Louis. Maybe I made a record or something or a date with him or something like that, but not too much. No, I didn't.

Well, you know, there seems to be -- a lot of people who knew him say that he was very -- the image that people have of him on the bandstand as being an Uncle Tom or something, that he wasn't like that off the bandstand at all.

Oh, no. Louis Armstrong was no Uncle Tom. He was just a guy doing to me as I would like -- no, doing to him as I would like for you to do unto me. But he tried to make everybody happy. Louis Armstrong was just a natural guy like that. Oh, he was wonderful. Too bad he died. But we all have to go sometime.
